# Dashboards {#sec-dashboards-chapter}

```{r setup}
#| echo: false
#| results: "asis"
source("prechapter.R")
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(webexercises))
insert_status_callout("incomplete")
```

A data dashboard is an interface to a dataset.

Typically:

* It provides a curated view of the most important summaries related to a particular question. (Such as graphs or summary statistics.)

* It fits on a single screen. (Dashboards are typically web pages.)

* It is interactive. (This can vary from small changes as the user moves their mouse across the dashboard, to allowing the user to customize what and how the data is summarized.)

Dashboards are a good way of distributing information to a less technical audience - however, a good dashboard requires some thought in its design.

In this chapter we will first consider the technical aspects of creating a dashboard, and then consider how to combine those into a good design.

## Formatting dashboards

We have already seen that R Markdown and Quarto files can be rendered to HTML files (i.e. web pages). However, these output files structure the content in a long vertical format that requires the user to scroll.

This works well for a long sequential report, but in a dashboard we want all the information to be visible on the screen at once. To do so we need to format the output webpage in a different style.

* R Markdown: we will use a package called `flexdashboard`.

  To do so, make sure the package is installed and then set the following line in your header section:
  
  ```md
  ---
  output: flexdashboard::flex_dashboard
  ---
  ```

* Quarto: we will use the built-in dashboard output, which is based on `flexdashboard`.

  To do so, change the `format` option in the header section to:
  
  ```md
  ---
  format: dashboard
  ---
  ```
